clinicalPearls: Internal tibial torsion is the commonest cause of in-toeing in toddlers and typically becomes apparent when the child begins to walk
The deformity is assessed on the rotational profile by the thigh-foot angle and the transmalleolar axis, with the child prone and the knee flexed
Tibial torsion normally shifts outward with growth, so mild internal torsion in infancy corrects to a modest external value by later childhood
The condition is usually physiological, frequently bilateral or asymmetrical, and resolves spontaneously without treatment in the great majority
Reassurance and observation are the mainstays, and passive stretching, special shoes, braces, and night splints have not been shown to alter the natural history
External tibial torsion is less common, tends to worsen with growth, and may contribute to patellofemoral maladjustment or an out-toeing gait
Surgical derotation osteotomy is reserved for the rare severe, persistent, and functionally significant deformity in an older child
reference.pathophysiology: Tibial torsion describes the normal axial rotation of the tibia between the knee and ankle, which in fetal life is internally rotated and gradually rotates externally through infancy and childhood as part of normal skeletal development. Persistence of the immature internally rotated pattern produces internal tibial torsion and an in-toeing gait, while excessive external rotation produces external torsion and out-toeing. It represents a variation of normal maturation influenced by intrauterine positioning and sleeping or sitting postures rather than a structural disease, and the growing bone remodels along the physiological path in the overwhelming majority of children.
additionalDifferentials: Increased femoral anteversion as an alternative cause of in-toeing
Metatarsus adductus producing in-toeing at the level of the foot
External tibial torsion or femoral retroversion causing out-toeing
Neuromuscular gait abnormality such as cerebral palsy
Blount disease or other tibial deformity mimicking torsional malalignment
additionalInvestigations: Full rotational profile assessment including thigh-foot angle and transmalleolar axis
Foot progression angle observed during gait
Assessment of hip rotation to exclude a coexisting femoral cause
Examination of the feet for metatarsus adductus or other deformity
Standing lower-limb radiographs only when angular deformity or a pathological cause is suspected
Computed tomography rotational study reserved for surgical planning in severe cases
redFlags: Progressive worsening rather than the expected spontaneous improvement
Marked asymmetry between the two limbs
Associated pain, limp, or functional limitation
Short stature, disproportion, or other features suggesting a skeletal dysplasia or metabolic bone disease
Neurological signs indicating an underlying neuromuscular disorder
reference.prognosis: The natural history is overwhelmingly benign, with internal tibial torsion resolving spontaneously in almost all children as the tibia derotates with growth, and lasting functional or arthritic consequences are not expected.
pitfalls: Prescribing braces, special shoes, or night splints that do not change the natural course and burden the family
Failing to complete a full rotational profile and thereby missing a coexisting femoral cause
Reassuring without follow-up when the deformity is progressive or asymmetrical
Attributing a pathological angular deformity such as Blount disease to simple torsion
Recommending surgery before the natural resolution that occurs with skeletal growth has been allowed
references: Staheli LT, rotational problems of the lower extremity
management: Reassure families and observe, as internal tibial torsion is physiological and resolves spontaneously in almost all children as the tibia derotates with growth
Avoid braces, night splints, special shoes and passive stretching, which do not alter the natural history
Monitor the rotational profile (thigh-foot angle and transmalleolar axis) over serial visits to confirm expected external derotation
Reserve derotational tibial osteotomy for the rare severe, persistent deformity causing functional or cosmetic problems in an older child
Follow external tibial torsion more closely, as it tends to worsen with growth and may contribute to patellofemoral maladjustment
Refer atypical, markedly asymmetrical, worsening or pathological cases to paediatric orthopaedics
